title: vpc-multihop-egress-strategy-proposal
content:
Purpose and context

This is a working proposal and workshop notes for a customer-facing POC that tests multi-hop VPC egress patterns for Redwood Private deployments. Customer wants deterministic outbound traffic control, split egress by data classification, and DNS behavior that preserves internal name resolution while allowing selective internet access for model downloads, telemetry, and third-party connectors. These notes capture constraints, proposed architectures, risk tradeoffs, a test plan, and an action checklist for the POC run.

Primary goals
- Provide deterministic, auditable egress paths for three traffic classes: private-only (no internet), restricted-internet (allowed outbound to curated endpoints), and open-internet (for model pulls during onboarding).
- Preserve private DNS resolution for internal hostnames and service discovery across peered VPCs.
- Keep latency for inference control plane calls under 60ms median when routed through any egress stack.
- Validate policy enforcement (IP allowlist, TLS intercept not desired) and logging for compliance.

Constraints and assumptions
- Customer environment: AWS-based VPCs with Transit Gateway available. Also trialing an on-prem datacenter with BGP-capable edge router.
- No TLS MITM; customer requires end-to-end TLS for external connectors.
- KMS/HSM integration required for key material; PV (private) deployment must not leave keys to Redwood-managed KMS.
- Expected peak QPS per VPC: 1,200 inference requests (control plane calls + telemetry) with short payloads.
- CIDR space: limited fragments; cannot re-IP large subnets for this POC.

Key customers risks to mitigate
- Misrouted egress leaking sensitive traffic to public internet.
- DNS resolution ambiguity between VPC peering and TGW attachment zones.
- Excessive latency from hairpinning through on-prem appliance.
- Operational complexity during blue/green cutovers (route table swaps).

Options considered (high-level)
Option A — TGW central egress + policy VPC (recommended for most customers)
- All VPCs attach to a Transit Gateway.
- A central policy VPC runs egress NATs, proxy fleet (optional), and DNS proxies.
- Route tables send 0.0.0.0/0 to TGW -> policy VPC; TGW enforces attachment isolation.
- Use AWS Network Firewall + Security Groups + Proxy allowlist for restricted-internet class.
Pros: single audit point, easier policy updates, scales with TGW.ASN.
Cons: potential hairpin latency, single point of egress failure if not multi-AZ.

Option B — Local egress with endpoint-centric S3/model downloads
- Each VPC uses local NAT Gateway or egress ENI.
- For model pulls and package downloads, use signed presigned URLs served by a private S3 or S3 Access Points with VPC endpoints.
- Restricted-internet allowed only via egress proxy deployed in each VPC as a sidecar/daemonset for cluster workloads.
Pros: lower latency for runtime calls, simpler routing.
Cons: policy drift across many VPCs and configuration sprawl.

Option C — Hybrid: TGW for telemetry & control plane; local egress for heavy model pulls
- Split flows by destination or port: control plane to Redwood-hosted endpoints goes via TGW + central proxy; large downloads hit S3 VPC endpoints directly to avoid egress charges and reduce cost.
- Use route tables with prefix lists to steer traffic.
Pros: cost/latency optimized.
Cons: more complex route table management and need for robust prefix-list automation.

DNS strategy (design details)
- Internal DNS namespace: keep private zone (example.internal.redwood) hosted in customer Route53 private hosted zone attached to all customer VPCs. Do not proxy internal names to public DNS.
- For central policy VPC (Option A), deploy a DNS forwarder (e.g., dnsmasq or BIND) that:
- For internal zones, forwards to Route53 via VPC resolver;
- For public resolution, forwards to provider resolvers but applies response policy zones (RPZ) for blocking known-bad domains.
- Encourage use of AWS Route53 Resolver inbound endpoints for on-prem integration and outbound endpoints for controlled public resolution.
- Ensure EDNS0 client-subnet not used in forward path to avoid geo-based resolution surprises.

Peering, routing, and BGP notes
- Prefer Transit Gateway for >2 VPC connectivity for scale and centralized route management.
- When connecting on-prem with BGP, avoid default route leakage; advertise only specific prefixes for service/control plane. Use BGP communities to tag learned routes for easier RBAC in TGW route tables.
- For direct VPC peering (if TGW not available), explicitly configure route tables to prevent overlapping CIDR issues; use DNS conditional forwarding to avoid split-brain.

Egress enforcement patterns and policy primitives
- IP allowlists maintained as AWS Prefix Lists and consumed by Security Groups and Network Firewall policies.
- Application allowlists: for TLS-only endpoints, use SNI-based allowlisting at proxy layer; fall back to IP allowlist when SNI is opaque (e.g., certificate pinning).
- Audit logs: flow logs to S3 -> Glue -> Athena for fast queries. Create an eventing pipeline for alerts on anomalies (e.g., egress to non-allowed IP).

Security and compliance controls
- No TLS intercept - ensure proxies operate in TCP passthrough when required.
- Mutual TLS for internal service-to-service connections where possible.
- KMS key material remains customer-managed in their KMS; Redwood services request ephemeral tokens.
- Harden NAT/proxy AMIs with CIS benchmarks and immutable image pipeline.

POC test plan (succinct tests with acceptance criteria)
1) Egress classification test
- Deploy three sample workloads that attempt: internal-only connection, restricted-internet (to curated analytics endpoint), and open-internet (download public model).
- Acceptance: restricted-internet allowed only to preconfigured domains; internal-only fails to reach internet; open-internet succeeds for presigned model fetch.
2) Latency impact test
- Run 1,200 QPS synthetic control plane calls through the egress path. Measure median and p95 latency.
- Acceptance: median < 60ms, p95 < 200ms.
3) DNS resolution fidelity test
- Ensure internal hostnames resolve correctly from all attached VPCs; validate there is no leakage to public DNS.
- Acceptance: all internal names resolve to private IPs; public names resolve externally.
4) Failover test
- Simulate central policy VPC AZ outage by removing route in one AZ; verify TGW reroutes to healthy AZ; verify no silent policy bypass.
- Acceptance: traffic remains consistent, and logs show routed path change.
5) Compliance logging test
- Trigger an attempt to access blocked domain and verify flow log entry, Network Firewall alert, and Slack webhook notification.
- Acceptance: all artifacts created and queryable within 5 minutes.

Operational runbook snippets (commands and checks)
- Quick health check: curl --resolve api.redwood.internal:443:<IP> https://api.redwood.internal/health -I
- Verify route table entry to TGW: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=route-table-id,Values=<rtb>
- Flow logs query (Athena): SELECT count(*) FROM vpc_flow_logs WHERE dstaddr = '1.2.3.4' AND action = 'REJECT' AND event_time > date_add('minute', -30, current_timestamp)

Open questions and TODOs
- Customer preference: central egress (Option A) vs hybrid (Option C)? Need cost model and traffic profile to decide.
- Determine who will operate image pipeline for proxy NAT AMIs (customer or Redwood).
- Decide retention window for egress flow logs (default 90 days vs 365 for compliance).
- Confirm whether any downstream connectors require explicit source IP stable ranges (if yes, we need static egress IP pool).

Workshop decisions captured
- Consensus to prototype Option C (hybrid) first for this POC: centralize control plane telemetry via TGW while routing large model downloads via VPC endpoints.
- Use AWS Prefix Lists for allowlists; customer to provide initial curated domain list.
- DNS design: Route53 private hosted zone + TGW-attached DNS forwarder for RPZ policy.

Next steps (owner/action/due)
- Asha: create Terraform skeleton for TGW attachments, prefix-lists, and route table automation (due 2025-11-10).
- Liam: build lightweight egress proxy AMI and publish test image to customer's sandbox account (due 2025-11-12).
- Priya: draft monitoring dashboard (cost, latency, blocked-egress events) and share with customer (due 2025-11-14).

Appendix: quick topology ASCII (simple)
Customer VPC A --\u003e TGW --\u003e Policy VPC (DNS forwarder + Network Firewall) --\u003e Internet
Customer VPC B --\u003e TGW --\u003e S3 VPC Endpoint (for model pulls)
On-prem site --BGP-- TGW (only advertise control prefixes)

Notes to self / meeting scribbles
- Customer asked about AWS PrivateLink for control plane: good for low-latency but requires endpoint services on our side; scope if they want hardened path.
- Consider implementing CIDR renumbering automation if customers have overlapping address space in future POCs.
- Keep an eye on AWS TGW long term costs vs many NAT gateways.

End of document
